title: EDRi-gram, 29 October 2026
content:
What has the EDRi network been up to over the past few weeks? Find out the latest digital rights news in our regular newsletter. In this edition: Celebrating end-to-end encryption, and the digital justice community in Europe and beyond

We’re still riding the high from October milestones showcasing the strength of our community. We had the pleasure of greeting many of you in person and online for #PrivacyCamp26 two weeks ago to discuss the origins of technology and how to pivot from conversations around “sovereignty” to meaningful, community-led self-determination. If you weren’t able to make it but you’re curious about the conversations, you can rewatch the livestream of some of the panel discussions.

Then, on October 21, we celebrated Global Encryption Day, highlighting end-to-end encryption as a crucial foundation to our right to safe and secure communication online and to life as we know it. Thanks to our members and partners, our message of protecting encryption was visible across several European capitals – from the metro trains of Prague to key landmarks in Berlin, Paris and Dublin with mobile “encryption trucks”. author: EDRi
title: The internet should not demand constant self-defence: Fairness starts before the click
content:
A fair digital environment cannot – and should not – depend on everyone being permanently alert. Fairness must be built into the environment itself, not left to the skills of the people using it. In practice, that means rules, not appeals: cancelling must be as easy as subscribing, protection must be the default rather than a setting, and a system that detects a moment of weakness must not be allowed to act on it.

You open an app to answer one message. Twenty minutes later, you are still there. A video starts playing before you choose it. The next one follows automatically. A notification appears just as you are about to leave. Cancelling a subscription takes six steps. Signing up took one.

We often blame these experiences on bad habits, weak self-control or poor digital literacy. That lets the companies designing them off the hook. The truth is that many digital services are built to keep us watching, clicking, buying and sharing data. They test colours, wording, timing, rankings and notifications to see what hooks us most. They learn when we hesitate, when we are tired and what makes us stay. The resulting pressure is rarely accidental: it is the business model. In 2019, EU consumer authorities made Booking.com change practices including misleading scarcity claims, discounts and rankings. Those messages telling us that a room is almost sold out are a reminder that interface design can manufacture urgency and push us toward a choice we might not otherwise have made.

This is why digital fairness cannot begin and end with the final click. By the time people press ‘accept’, ‘buy’ or ‘continue’, the service may already have shaped the options, concealed the alternatives and created the urgency.

The usual language of consumer choice assumes a roughly equal encounter between a company and an informed individual. Online, that assumption collapses. The company has the data, the designers, the behavioural research and the power to adjust the environment in real time. What do we have? A small screen, limited time and no access to the logic shaping what we see.

A fair digital environment cannot – and should not – depend on everyone being permanently alert. No one can examine every default, decode every recommendation system, or resist every strategically timed prompt. Fairness must be built into the environment itself, not left to the skills of the people using it. In practice, that means rules, not appeals: cancelling must be as easy as subscribing, protection must be the default rather than a setting, and a system that detects a moment of weakness must not be allowed to act on it.

That also changes how we think about vulnerability. Policy often treats vulnerability as a fixed characteristic of particular groups. Yet digital systems do not wait for vulnerable groups. In fact, they can create vulnerable moments and then act on them. Anyone becomes easier to influence when tired, lonely, rushed, financially stressed or overwhelmed. Someone browsing late at night, hesitating over a purchase or repeatedly returning to the same offer may be easier to influence in that moment. A digital service can detect those signals and adapt what it shows next. Of course, some people and groups face these pressures far more often, and with harsher consequences. But the wider point matters: vulnerability is shaped by design, context and power, not only by who a person is.

There is a collective dimension too. It is tempting to say that no one has to use these services. But increasingly, that is no longer true: what was once a choice is becoming an obligation, as public services, healthcare or social support require people to interact with digital systems they did not choose and cannot easily avoid. And even where the choice remains, it exists only one person at a time. One person may be able to close an app, reject a prompt or pay for a different service. A whole society cannot. It cannot simply opt out of digital systems that organise communication, work, culture and access to information.

When the same commercial incentives shape the services used by millions of people, the effects do not stay private. They quietly decide what becomes visible, what disappears, which voices travel further and which forms of behaviour come to seem normal. Digital fairness therefore concerns how we live together, not only the quality of individual transactions.

For me, the promise of digital fairness is not better self-defence, but less need for it: it is a society that places limits on how companies may influence us. Self-determination should not mean another dashboard full of settings. It should mean that cancelling takes as many steps as signing up: one. It should mean being able to use a service without every hesitation becoming a signal, every pause becoming a cue to intervene and every moment of weakness becoming commercially useful. It should mean that refusing profiling or constant engagement is not punished with a worse service or social exclusion.

The debate goes beyond a few irritating interfaces. Design choices shape which prices people see, which opportunities reach them at all and how difficult it becomes to leave. What is at stake is not convenience but access to information, equality, data protection and participation. These are questions of power, even when they appear as ordinary product decisions.

That means better design alone will never be enough. Companies may improve a button while keeping the same objective behind it: collect more data, hold attention for longer and make exit less likely. A fairer interface can still sit on top of an unfair system. The real test is what a service is optimising for, who benefits when it works and who bears the cost. Otherwise, ‘user-friendly’ can become another word for frictionless extraction. And friction is sometimes exactly what protects us.

Europe increasingly talks about reducing technological dependencies. That matters, as long as we frame it correctly. Because origin is a poor proxy for fairness: replacing a foreign platform with an EU one achieves little if the new service relies on the same extraction, profiling and behavioural pressure. Any serious project of digital self-determination must therefore ask more than who owns the technology, it must ask which business model it serves, who can shape it and what limits apply to its power. Without digital fairness, sovereignty risks becoming a change of supplier rather than a change in power.

A fair digital future should not demand that every person becomes an expert in seeing through manipulation but should make manipulative design a bad business strategy.

First published on Feminist Tech Policy, a project by SUPERRR

author: EDRi
title: What the new Convention on Decent Work in the Platform Economy means for workers – and what’s next for implementation
content:
In June 2026, the International Labour Organisation (ILO) adopted a new Convention on Decent Work in the Platform Economy. Following in the footsteps of the EU’s Platform Work Directive, this Convention extends data protection rights for platform workers and contains innovative provisions to protect against the adverse effects of automated decision-making globally. But this is only the beginning. In this article, EDRi member Privacy International explores what’s next for ratification, implementation and the future of regulating worker surveillance in the EU and around the world.

By Privacy International (guest author) · October 29, 2026

On 12 June 2026, the International Labour Organisation (ILO) adopted Convention C193 on Decent Work in the Platform Economy. This is a landmark piece of legislation as the first global legally binding instrument regulating the platform economy and addressing the impact of technology on the world of work.

The Convention represents a significant step forward for workers’ rights around the globe. It reflects the growing consensus that digital platform workers need more adequate protection from abusive and exploitative employment practices. It also reflects the need to regulate the use of automated decision-making (ADM) in the workplace affecting platform workers, an issue Privacy International has developed a set of recommendations on.

Covering similar ground to the EU’s Platform Work Directive, the Convention contains provisions on: fairer compensation, extension of access to certain social protections, the right to collective bargaining, improved occupational health and safety standards, and data protection rights to access, rectify and erase their personal data.

Crucially, the Convention recognises the need for greater transparency in algorithmic management. Section X requires companies to inform workers about the use of automated systems in monitoring their performance, allocating tasks and making decisions affecting their work and access to work. It also gives workers the right to request written explanations of significant automated decisions, as well as request review of decisions that negatively impact them. While more is needed, this sets a new global standard and expectation, codifying the reality that platform workers are indeed workers – rather than merely contractors with platforms as the intermediaries.

The next step is ensuring that governments properly implement and adequately enforce the Convention. While the Convention provides historical gains for workers, the text is not perfect; some language around the automated decision-making provisions default to vague terms. For instance, rather than hard-edged requirements, States are only obliged to ‘take appropriate measures’ to ensure responsible use of ADM, and worker access to written explanations pertains only to ‘significant’ decisions. As the deadline for transposition of the Platform Work Directive nears, this fight for strong implementation of platform workers’ rights will spread around the world.

As States approach national implementation, they must ensure that they clearly articulate the nature of those ‘appropriate measures’ in a bold and ambitious way.

At minimum, States should push for platforms to provide explanations of decisions to workers by default, rather than just ‘upon request’. Explanations should also be specific and personalised to the worker, specifying the data and parameters on which decisions are based, and how an alternative outcome could have been reached. States should also consider how platforms can give workers and their representatives access to APIs, sandboxes or source code to understand for themselves how the algorithms work.

It is also essential that references to classification of employment not be interpreted to undermine the Convention’s practical effectiveness; all workers in the platform economy, regardless of their employment status, should enjoy the rights afforded by the Convention.

Governments, platforms and the ILO should engage directly with workers, union representatives and civil society to develop effective legislative frameworks and adequate enforcement that best serve the rights and interests of workers. The ILO should also revisit a non-binding recommendation that was meant to be adopted alongside Convention C193. The draft Recommendation provided more detail on issues like transparency and explainability, giving essential guidance to Member States and platforms to support them in their interpretation of the Convention provisions. The delay to this recommendation creates the opportunity for it to respond to lessons learned in implementation and new emerging practices.

Convention C193 has laid the groundwork that recognises the impact digital technology is having on platform workers around the world. But the issue is of course not limited to the platform economy. In late 2025, the European Parliament passed a resolution calling for a more general legislative proposal on algorithmic management in the workplace – and both the European Commission and the ILO have conducted research into the use of automated systems beyond the platform economy.

Privacy International have been working with fellow advocates from trade unions, digital rights organisations and human rights organisations to push for a strong ILO Convention, and together we must continue to fight for stronger safeguards for workers against the harms of automated decision-making in other spaces and forums.

author: EDRi
title: Draconian access block orders in Turkey
content:
Court orders to block access to X accounts in Turkey reached an unprecedented number in September 2026. In this blog, EDRi-member Alternatif Bilisim detail the crackdown on civil rights defenders and independent media in the country, and call on public authorities to reconsider block orders and protect fundamental rights.

By Alternatif Bilisim (guest author) · October 29, 2026

Court orders to block access to X accounts in Turkey reached an unprecedented number in September 2026, followed by the closure of T24, an independent news website. According to data from the EngelliWeb project of the Freedom of Expression Association (İFÖD), X blocked at least 1,270 accounts. In comparison, a total of 995 accounts were blocked in the entire year of 2025. In fact, the website of EngelliWeb, which tracks and documents online censorship in Turkey, was also blocked on 1 October 2026. Authoritarian measures and alarming levels of censorship in the country are increasingly eroding freedom of expression.

The common factor in all decisions related to access block orders is Article 8/A of Law No. 5651. This article allows the right of life, the safety of life and property of the persons, the protection of national security and public order, the prevention of crime or the protection of the internet contents or the prevention of access to the internet content. Several restrictions on access blocks in September cited grounds such as national security or protection of public order under 8/A.

Article 8/A was introduced by the government as an arrangement that was supposed to be implemented in exceptional cases, but its use has been gradually expanding. The use of this article is also being combined with the new provisions on family values under the so-called “My Family is Safe” investigations, which have led to a brutal crackdown on LGBTQ+ and HIV advocacy groups in Turkey.

EDRi-member Alternatif Bilisim condemns this act by the Turkish authorities and the complicity of X on the shadow bans. Turkey is increasingly witnessing an ideological surge on critical opinion and its clear consequences for the journalism landscape as well as digital spaces at large.

According to Engelliweb, in September 2026, many different accounts – from LGBTQ+ organisations and activists to journalists, academics to economists, from women’s organisations to individual users – were impacted by the access blocks. A few examples of note are the accounts of Evrensel, a socialist newspaper; Amnesty International Turkey; Academics for Peace; and the Media and Law Studies Association.

In the second half of September, social media posts on capital markets have also a key focus of blocks due to alleged cause of fear and panic in the society. A major capital-markets scandal in Turkey involved widespread market manipulation by asset managers who allegedly inflated fund values using worthless “junk stocks,” leading to the liquidation of 131 funds and affecting about 455,000 investors. Authorities arrested over 114 people and froze assets as part of the investigation into fraud and criminal organization charges.

A more recent disproportionate measure has been the closure of a prominent independent news website T24 and its social media accounts after the justice ministry reported that they had published 118 items during the previous year which the court classified as “LGBTQ propaganda”. The X accounts of Independent News Network Bianet, as well as several of its reporters have also been banned due to court orders citing national security and protection of public order.

Court decisions on access to an account does not mean that the account will automatically become invisible in X from Turkey. The decision must also be implemented by the platform. X did not implement all the decisions. According to the IFÖD’s findings, 1,139 of the at least 1,270 accounts (around 90 percent) that were blocked in September were made invisible from Turkey by X. According to X’s official policy, the company can only block access to certain content or accounts in the respective country when it receives a valid and appropriate legal request from an competent authority. The account is not closed globally in this case. Co-founder of EngelliWeb, Yaman Akdeniz, argues that platforms have become more harmonious with the demands of the authorities in Turkey, especially after March 19, 2025, following the arrest of Istanbul mayor and presidential candidate of the main opposition party (CHP), Ekrem Imamoglu along with 100+ opposition members due to alleged corruption and aid to terrorists.

While ideologically-oriented access block decisions lack legitimacy, legal grounds manufactured for such decisions should be subject to scrutiny. Transparency is also significant because in some cases, users have not been notified by X about the blocking of their accounts unless inquired by the user or legal experts.

Alternatif Bilisim calls on public authorities in Turkey to reconsider block orders based on full account bans rather than single posts and to immediately lift bans targeting a wide community of rights defenders, journalists and news websites as part of the so-called “My Family is Safe” investigation. Delegating the responsibility to the Constitutional Court mostly delays the process for up to 5 years; thus such disproportionate practices of censorship create chilling effects and should be eliminated.

Alternatif Bilisim also appeals to digital rights organisations in Europe and beyond to flag such rights violations to hold governments responsible and social media platforms accountable.

As a digital rights organisation with 15 years of experience in the digital rights field, Alternatif Bilisim will continue monitoring such violations and keep on forming alliances with civil society in the media and journalism field. They also plan to create wider public awareness on non-extractive social-sharing platforms.

author: EDRi
title: Surveillance in times of insecurity: a wicked and stupid strategy
content:
Sweden has been grappling with crime-related challenges in the past years. The difficulty to address violent crimes in cities notably has triggered extensive legislative reforms to increase surveillance and repression, including that of children. Tougher criminal penalties, widespread videosurveillance, mass electronic monitoring and government hacking are just a few examples illustrating the Swedish government’s attempt to counter public safety threats.

Sweden has been grappling with crime-related challenges in the past years. The difficulty to address violent crimes in cities notably has triggered extensive legislative reforms to increase surveillance and repression, including that of children. Tougher criminal penalties, widespread video surveillance, mass electronic monitoring and government hacking are just a few examples illustrating the Swedish government’s attempt to counter public safety threats.

However, this approach is not only misguided, as no evidence of its effectiveness exists, but also harmful to the fundamental right to personal integrity and thus to Swedish democracy. Furthermore, its impacts disproportionately fall on communities already marginalised and overpoliced.

Personal integrity is a key principle firmly embedded in the Swedish constitution. Between 2004 and 2017, the Swedish government tasked several inquiry committees to assess the impacts of new technologies on democracy and privacy, which led to important constitutional amendments reinforcing protections. And for very good reasons. The right to privacy ensures the respect and protection of people’s self-determination and their freedom of expression, assembly and association, the exercise of which is a sine qua non for democratic societies.

Privacy is neither a luxury nor a niche concern to the most computer-savvy. Examples of data breach, abuse and exploitation show how people lose power when their data, communications, movements, and associations are captured, monitored and exploited. In the digital age, nobody has “nothing to hide”.

In 2020 the New York Times revealed that the US company Clearview AI had amassed a database of billions of photos of people’s faces by scraping them from social media without their knowledge or consent, in order to provide a facial recognition tool to police forces. Clearview’s tool was used by hundreds of law enforcement agencies across the world, including in Sweden where the Data Protection Authority had to intervene to stop and sanction the unlawful processing of people’s sensitive biometric data. Whether you chose for your face to appear online or not, it is crucial for your right to privacy and for a flourishing and open Internet where you can freely express yourself that no private company steals your photos and shares all that information with the police for no valid reason.

For some categories of the population, privacy is even a lifeline. In 2023, a mother and her daughter were convicted for allegedly carrying out an illegal abortion in the US after Facebook transferred their private conversation on Messenger to the police. This case example underlines the importance of minimising the amount of user data internet companies should be able to access and store, especially in a context of increasing restrictions imposed on reproductive rights in many countries. Services offering access to safe abortion rely on secure and private communication channels, such as encrypted platforms, to protect themselves and their patients against multiple threats.

Privacy enables autonomy, dissent, and democratic participation. It acts as a shield when activists, journalists and even ordinary people get criminalised. If privacy goes down, all rights start falling like dominoes. Protecting our collective and personal boundaries today preserves freedom tomorrow.

Surveillance measures to tackle insecurity are doomed to fail. They are usually sold by politicians as quick technological fixes to complex societal issues. Yet, they are never backed up by robust evidence to prove their efficiency.

The presumption that videosurveillance cameras in public spaces help investigations or contribute to reducing crime rates has long been debunked by research studies. In 2016, the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) declared the Swedish regime of mass retention of telecommunications data illegal under European Union (EU) law because the Court found no objective evidence supporting the fact that putting everyone under surveillance, regardless if they are suspect or not, was necessary to combat criminal offences.

Not to mention the huge side-effect of increased digital vulnerabilities. The more the government collects and stores people’s data for surveillance purposes, the more personal data becomes a prey to cybercriminals. Cyberattacks linked to the Chinese government that compromised US critical infrastructures and telecommunications networks demonstrate how government-mandated vulnerabilities in digital systems can quickly backfire for the population.

Worse still, surveillance measures can have disastrous consequences and generate more public safety problems. In 2021, the Dutch, Belgian and French police revealed that they had infiltrated and shut down the encrypted communication network named “Sky ECC” to target drug trafficking criminal groups. They secretly collected and analysed millions of messages exchanged, leading to mass arrests across the continent. However, a study commissioned by the European Commission found that “not only has the Sky ECC operation failed to reduce violent crime rates in Belgium and the Netherlands, but the displacement of cocaine shipping routes provoked by disruptive law enforcement methods may have contributed to rising violence in areas which are increasingly exploited by [organised crime groups] seeking new avenues to import cocaine into Europe“. The bulk hacking of the platform simply displaced the problem of violence geographically: the operation had even contributed to a slight increase in homicide rate in Belgium and created new cocaine import hotspots to the detriment of local residents in the impacted neighbourhoods.

Surveillance is the symptom of repressive and punitive approaches to societal challenges, which consistently fail to properly address them. Although they give an appearance of security, they don’t actually contribute to increasing real-life security. People working on the frontline of these issues, such as marginalised youth alienation, know that other solutions are needed, and those are not to be found in the criminal justice field.

Issues faced by Sweden, like other EU countries, are understandably tough to solve. But using more surveillance and control, thus undermining privacy, is elected officials shirking their job and attempting to score political points. Instead, they should tackle safety issues at their root causes: growing socioeconomic disparities, poverty, lack of opportunities, lost sense of community belonging, racism in institutions, etc.

Rather than undermining our rights, we should work towards finding measures that reinforce our care systems, our collective accountability, our dignity, our connections to each other, and our universal right to live freely. That is exactly what should be understood by Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson when he called for “the collective power of society” to reduce violent crime, surveillance is not.

This article was first published in Swedish by the Liberal Debatt.

author: EDRi
title: EDRi celebrates Global Encryption Day 2026
content:
On 21 October 2026, we celebrate the Global Encryption Day! Part of EDRi’s KISS campaign, we celebrate this day with our partners, online, in Brussels and in different European capitals.

On 21 October 2026, we celebrate the Global Encryption Day! Part of EDRi’s KISS campaign, we celebrate this day with our partners, online, in Brussels and in different European capitals.

A recent survey conducted by CDT Europe shows that across several European countries (France, Sweden, Poland, and Ireland), people consistently oppose measures that would compromise encrypted communication platforms. In France, 92% of respondents agree they have the right to have private conversations online, while the figure goes to 94% in Poland, 88% in Sweden and 93% in Ireland.

Encryption is great for protecting the way our messages travel on the internet. Through “end to end encryption”, anyone can make sure that the content of an online conversation can not be intruded upon, not even the server that facilitates the transmission.

This year, we have coordinated several campaign actions to celebrate encryption.

1. Raising awareness in European Capitals through LED “Encryption trucks” driving around Paris, Berlin and Dublin and a metro poster campaign in Prague.

To visibilise people’s support for encryption, we partnered with the Irish Council for Civil Liberties, Féministes contre le cyberharcèlement and Digitale Gesellschaft who are in the streets today, talking to people and press about the “Encryption trucks” and the importance of encryption. In Prague, our partner Iure has been supporting the Metro Posters campaign for the past weeks.

2. Working across silos with groups promoting gender justice, and sex workers rights in the digitalised society.

In the case of women defenders, land defenders from indigenous groups, racial justice activists, sex workers defenders and defenders of migrants, unsafe communications can have life or death consequences. For human rights defenders, secure and trusted communication is often a matter of physical safety and democratic organising.

For 21 October 2026, we have partnered with European Sex Workers Alliance and Féministes contre le cyberharcèlement (France) to raise awareness on the importance of safe and secure communications for sex workers as well as womens’ rights. Check ESWA’s Instagram video and

3. Visibilising the testimonials of activists from Privacy Camp and across Europe

During 14th edition of Privacy Camp gathering that happened recently in Brussels, EDRi asked a few participants why encryption mattered for them. The people we interviewed came from a variety of causes: those fighting for a healthy European civic space, and for digital rights in Netherlands, Portugal and Germany. More, we asked EDRi’s over 35.000 supporters why encryption mattered to them too. Their answers inspired us to post some of them, and we will post them during the next couple of weeks. Check the content on EDRi’s social media channels – on Instagram , Mastodon or LinkedIn.

4. Connecting with global experts to advocate for encryption

During the Global Encryption Summit taking place at 4pm CET, EDRi’s expert Chloé Berthélémy will join a panel in an event organised by Internet Society, the Center for Democracy and Technology, Mozilla, and Global Partners Digital.

Europol and law enforcement are pushing to legalise hacking methods that weaken encryption. These methods rely on ordering a service provider (those who develop or maintain the software, computer system, network, or electronic device) to build vulnerabilities in their systems. With this demand, state actors want to enable the police or intelligence agencies to have access to our data and break encryption. Client-side scanning (scanning of all content such as text,images, videos, etc. on a device or shared in a communication channel) is a method proposed under the EU CSA Regulation. Key escrows or “key recovery”, involves placing decryption keys in a “vault” managed by a trusted authority or group of trusted authorities, who can break them out when access to the encrypted data is needed. Finally, ghost proposals refer to the modification of the encryption system to enable a third-party listener to be silently added to encrypted conversations.

In democratic societies, communication systems are vital for our lives and connections with others. Safe and secure communications and devices allow us to work, socialise, organise, express ourselves, and connect with each other.

author: Chiara Miraglia
title: CPDP 20th international conference
content:
CPDP (“Computers, Privacy and Data Protection”) is a non-profit platform founded in 2007 by research groups at the Vrije Universiteit Brussel, the Université de Namur, and Tilburg University, later joined by INRIA and the Fraunhofer Institute for Systems and Innovation Research. Today, CPDP is carried by 20 academic centres of excellence from the EU, the US, and beyond. Based in Brussels, CPDP has become a world-leading multidisciplinary conference, convening a global community across research, policy, practice, civil society, and technology to engage with cutting-edge developments in privacy and data protection.

Organiser: 20 academic centres of excellence from the EU, the US, and beyond

The governance of the digital world is fragmented and faces difficult challenges. Technologies that shape our lives develop faster than the means – or even the will – to regulate them for the protection of privacy and other fundamental rights.

What We Owe the Future invites reflection on this contribution. Building on this, it looks ahead to what the future demands of us. What will the next twenty or more years need, and how should we help to build it? What do we owe to those who will inherit the world we shape today? author: EDRi
title: EDRi-gram, 8 October 2026
content:
What has the EDRi network been up to over the past few weeks? Find out the latest digital rights news in our regular newsletter. In this edition: Turning up the heat – Commission backs social media bans, Apple held accountable, summer to-dos, & more!

This EDRi-gram edition includes a real snapshot of the disconnect between the kind of technology and protections people and communities around the world need, and the kind that are being pushed at us by lawmakers and companies either for the sake of profits, as easy fixes to structural societal issues or more sinister reasons.

Take the EU’s recently announced KIDS ACT. We unpack the many shortcomings of the proposal which is a missed opportunity to address the root cause of why online platforms are harmful to children – and everyone else. We also look at the Cloud and AI Development (CADA) Act, a part of the EU’s Tech Sovereignty Package announced earlier this year. What was sold as a way to jumpstart the EU’s “sovereign AI” ambitions seems to be set to hurt digital rights and environmental protections instead, while also imposing an unreliable technology onto us.

Elsewhere, Austria will soon get to find out what happens when AI systems are allowed to issue legally binding government decisions without any human oversight. EDRi-member epicenter.works detail the draft proposal and all the ways it could backfire.

None of the above

author: EDRi
title: The Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA) represents everything that’s wrong with Europe’s approach to digital sovereignty
content:
The EU’s Tech Sovereignty Package is supposed to jump-start Europe’s “sovereign AI” ambitions. But due to fundamental misunderstandings about the technology behind ‘AI’ and the blind trust in Big Tech’s AI doomer and boomer narratives, it is more likely to instead hurt digital rights and the environment instead, and waste valuable public resources that should have been invested in actually increasing Europe’s digital resilience. The Cloud and AI Development (CADA) Act, a part of the Tech Sovereignty Package, adds up to an aggressive policy push to impose “European AI”.

Published on 3 June, the European Commission’s Tech Sovereignty Package—comprising the Chips Act 2.0, the Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA), the EU Open Source Strategy, and a Strategic Roadmap for Energy Digitalisation—is portrayed as a significant shift in the EU’s digital governance strategy. It signals that the EU is no longer content to rely on regulatory frameworks like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), Digital Services Act (DSA), Digital Markets Act (DMA) and the Artificial Intelligence (AI) Act. The EU now seeks to artificially inflate both the supply of and demand for AI data centres, as well as to expand the material infrastructures underpinning them.

author: EDRi
title: No human required: Austria’s plan for AI-only government decisions
content:
A sweeping change to Austria's administrative law would let authorities issue binding decisions using AI systems with no human ever reviewing the outcome. EDRi member epicenter.works has sent an open letter to parliament, and is looking for input from readers elsewhere in Europe about how other countries are handling, or planning to handle, the same issue.

By epicenter.works (guest author) · October 8, 2026

Austria is about to find out what happens when a member state lets large language models write legally binding government decisions, with no human required to review them.

This autumn, the Constitutional Affairs Committee of Austria’s parliament will debate a sweeping change to the country’s General Administrative Procedure Act (AVG). The AVG is the default procedural code for essentially all administrative proceedings in Austria, covering everything from social assistance and building permits to business licensing and public subsidies. A single change to the general code can therefore affect how decisions get made across almost the entire administration, not just in one sector. author: EDRi
title: Your data, their decision: the hidden surveillance infrastructure behind Europe’s digital borders
content:
A new report by ARTICLE 19 examines how the European Union is presiding over the most significant expansion of border surveillance in its history. Much of this development is being outsourced to private companies – with profound consequences for privacy and freedom of expression.

By ARTICLE 19 (guest author) · October 8, 2026

In October 2025, the EU began systematically collecting and storing fingerprints and facial images of every third-country national crossing its external border, under the Entry/Exit System (EES). By late 2026, the European Travel Information and Authorisation System (ETIAS) will expand this approach by pre-screening visa-exempt travellers before they arrive at EU borders.

Together, the two systems are capable of processing more than 1.4 billion travellers, integrating biometric, migration, visa, and law-enforcement data into searchable profiles.

The new report by ARTICLE 19, examining how the EU is significantly expanding border surveillance, focuses on the agency at the heart of the system: EU-LISA (EU Agency for the Operational Management of Large-Scale IT Systems in the Area of Freedom, Security and Justice). This little-scrutinised entity plays a key role in building and maintaining the large-scale digital infrastructure projects that underpin EU migration and border management.

author: EDRi
title: D3 brings class actions on addictive design against Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and YouTube
content:
The Portuguese digital rights organisation and EDRi member D3 announces that it has brought four class actions lawsuits against Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and YouTube over the use of addictive design practices. The cases challenge design practices that can encourage compulsive use of online platforms and seek to hold platforms accountable for the way their services affect users. Similar initiatives might come up in other EU Member States as part of a broader European response.

By D3 – Defesa dos Direitos Digitais & NOVA School of Law (guest author) · October 8, 2026

In April and May 2026, D3 brought four cases before the Portuguese civil courts against Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and YouTube. The proceedings took the form of a “popular action”, that is, a specific legal mechanism for collective redress provided for in the Portuguese Constitution in which D3 acts as a collective representative of the rights of people in Portugal.

The cases concern the business models of major platforms and the incentives created by the attention economy. D3 argues that the platforms’ business models should not depend on design mechanisms that undermine users’ ability to exercise control over their own use of digital services.

The purpose of the actions is to seek greater accountability from platforms and to ensure that users can have a safer experience online.

author: EDRi
title: The KIDS Act will make the internet less safe
content:
On 16 September, the European Commission presented the KIDS ACT, its plan for making online experiences safer for young people. Far from being a move to lead the EU towards better digital environments, this move is a missed opportunity to address the root cause of why online platforms are harmful to children – and everyone else. This blog analyse the proposal’s shortcomings.

During her annual address to the European Parliament, the President of the European Commission announced her intention to protect young people from platforms and services that deprive children of their childhood and of their focus. The next day, the Commission published the KIDS ACT (an acronym for ‘Keeping Internet Digital Spaces Accountable and Trustworthy’). This announcement arrives after a period of much debate around protecting young people online, and even announcements of social media bans from countries across Europe. As a response to this discussion, on April 22, youth organisations across Europe came together to demand real change, instead of exclusions and bans, from EU lawmakers.

The Commission had the opportunity to change the rules of the dangerous game that makes people unsafe online. Instead, it’s mostly restricting who gets to play.
